paras: The attempted lynching at Rayville, Louisiana, took place on or shortly before August 4, 1905, when a mob of about 100 armed men took a Black man from a Vicksburg, Shreveport and Pacific train and prepared to hang him. He was released after the husband of the woman he was accused of slapping said he was innocent; northern papers presented it as lynchers acting on rumor.

According to a New Orleans dispatch, the mob dragged the man, who is not named, from the train at Rayville and was about to hang him to a nearby tree. The mob accused him of having slapped a white woman, Mrs. Allen Sholars, at Monroe. Someone noted that Mr. Sholars was on the train and could say what had happened.

When found, Sholars said it was "all a mistake": in a scrimmage at the Monroe station his nurse had been knocked down, "probably by the police" making an arrest, and the man was "entirely innocent of any offense." The man was then allowed to leave on the train, which the dispatch described as "paralyzed by fright at his narrow escape from lynching."
No report of arrests or other action against the mob appears in the coverage.

Every paper found ran the same New Orleans wire dispatch nearly word for word. The New York Sun printed it on August 5 under the headline "Lynching Fever in Louisiana," with the subhead "A Mob About to Hang a Negro for an Offense He Didn't Commit." The same day the New Haven Union headed it "Negro Escapes Rope," saying he "Proves His Innocence to the Necktie Party," and spelled the family name "Scholars."

On August 6 the Washington Evening Star quoted the dispatch and added an editorial comment that the "little busy lyncher" embellished each rumor and that "his interest in facts is secondary where it exists at all." The Star added that such a man, shown an accused person, "a negro preferred," was ready with a rope or gun at once. No Louisiana paper and no Black newspaper report of the episode was found.

reader.title: Attempted lynching at Rayville, Louisiana (1905)
bases: An armed mob seized a Black man from a train and was about to hang him, then released him (A1, A3); an attempted lynching.

A mob of 100 armed men, acting without legal authority on the accusation that the man had slapped a white woman, was about to hang him, but he was released alive (A1, A3); no one was killed, so it was an attempted lynching.
All three papers print the same New Orleans wire dispatch nearly word for word (A1, A2, A3); no independent local or Black-press report was found.

accounts.label: Mr. Sholars's statement (as reported in the dispatch)

framing.detail: The Sun ran the dispatch under 'Lynching Fever in Louisiana. A Mob About to Hang a Negro for an Offense He Didn't Commit.'
The New Haven Union headed it 'Negro Escapes Rope: Proves His Innocence to the Necktie Party in Louisiana.'
The Evening Star quoted the dispatch and commented that the lyncher's 'interest in facts is secondary' and that he is ready with a rope for any accused man, 'a negro preferred.'
